title: Behavioral rehabilitation of extremely fearful dogs: Report on the efficacy of a treatment protocol
authors: Collins K, Miller K, Zverina L, Patterson-Kane E, Cussen V, Reid P
abstract: Some dogs entering shelters exhibit extreme fearfulness, often after experiencing cruelty or neglect. Dogs displaying extreme fearfulness are difficult to assess and treat using the tools and protocols available in most shelters. Without effective treatment, these dogs have an unacceptably poor quality of life and are unlikely to be successfully adopted. Treatment protocols using behavior modification techniques such as desensitization, counterconditioning and operant conditioning were developed to reduce fear of stimuli that pet dogs typically experience in adoptive homes. From 2013–2020, outcomes were recorded for dogs that went through this behavioral rehabilitation program. The graduation rate from the program was 86 % (380/441). Graduated dogs spent an average of 96 (SD=55) days in the program, experiencing an average of 78 specific treatment sessions. They showed a significant improvement in behavior in a standardized behavior assessment (df=440, t = 28.3836, p = 0.001) before meeting criteria for placement. Once offered for adoption, they had a 99 % adoption rate and a 96 % adopter satisfaction rate. These results indicate that an appropriately designed behavioral rehabilitation program for dogs displaying extreme fear in a shelter setting can prove highly successful, resulting in improved quality of life and reduced need for behavioral euthanasia.

mcqs.q: In the ASPCA Behavioral Rehabilitation Center study (Collins et al. 2022), what was the graduation rate from the behavioral rehabilitation program for extremely fearful shelter dogs?
mcqs.e: The abstract states: 'The graduation rate from the program was 86 % (380/441).' The 99% figure refers to the adoption rate among graduates, not graduation from the program.

mcqs.q: According to Collins et al. 2022, which behavior modification techniques were central to the ASPCA behavioral rehabilitation protocol for extremely fearful shelter dogs?
o: A) Flooding, positive punishment, and operant conditioning
B) Desensitization, counterconditioning, and operant conditioning
C) Systematic desensitization alone with no food reinforcement
D) Response substitution and differential reinforcement of incompatible behavior only
mcqs.e: The abstract explicitly names 'desensitization, counterconditioning and operant conditioning' as the core techniques used to reduce fear of stimuli that pet dogs typically encounter in adoptive homes.

mcqs.q: The Collins et al. 2022 study found that graduated dogs had a significant improvement in standardized behavior assessment scores before placement. What does this finding most directly support regarding shelter behavioral rehabilitation programs?
o: A) All extremely fearful shelter dogs should be immediately euthanized due to poor prognosis
B) Simple enrichment and time in the shelter environment alone are sufficient to rehabilitate extremely fearful dogs
C) An appropriately designed behavioral rehabilitation program can significantly reduce fear and improve adoption outcomes even for the most fearful dogs
D) Psychopharmacology alone without behavior modification is adequate for fearful dog rehabilitation
mcqs.e: The abstract concludes: 'an appropriately designed behavioral rehabilitation program for dogs displaying extreme fear in a shelter setting can prove highly successful, resulting in improved quality of life and reduced need for behavioral euthanasia.' The paper also showed that time in environment without treatment (delayed-onset group) was insufficient—behavior modification protocols specifically drove improvement.

title: Too much too soon? Risk factors for fear behaviour in foster kittens prior to adoption
authors: Graham C, Pearl DL, Niel L
abstract: Many companion kittens spend their sensitive period for socialization (~2–9 weeks of age) in foster care, and the quality of these early life experiences can impact behavioural development. This study aimed to improve early kitten care by using an online survey to investigate risk factors for fear behaviour in foster kittens prior to adoption (7–9 weeks of age) based on early management practices, foster parent personality traits, and evaluations of kitten behaviour. The main behavioural outcomes of this study were whether kittens showed caregiver-reported fear behaviour during interactions with unfamiliar people and unfamiliar objects just prior to adoption. Fear behaviour included displays of avoidance, freezing, crouching, ears back, piloerection, and aggression. We analyzed the impacts of kitten (n=235) and foster parent (n=72) characteristics, exposure to social stimuli (i.e., general handling, mimicking handling during a vet visit, exposure to people), and exposure to non-social stimuli (e.g., interactive toys, scratching material, different surfaces, etc.) provided. Using mixed logistic regression models, with foster parent as a random intercept to account for clustering at the foster home level, we found that kittens who were reported fearful at intake into foster care had significantly greater odds of displaying fear behaviours towards unfamiliar people and unfamiliar objects than kittens who were not reported fearful at intake. Additionally, kittens who received exposure to cognitive enrichment-based non-social stimuli had greater odds of displaying fear towards people compared to kittens who did not receive cognitive exposure. Kittens whose foster parent had a high score for emotional stability had greater odds of displaying fear towards people compared to those who had a low score for emotional stability. Further, kittens who received high exposure to social stimuli had reduced odds of displaying fear towards people than kittens who received low social exposure, as predicted. Some of these findings challenge recommendations for high amounts of exposure to social and non-social stimuli during early socialization. High social exposure was ineffective at reducing fear levels towards unfamiliar objects, and high cognitive enrichment-based non-social exposure appears to have exceeded kitten limits for optimal behavioural development. While appropriate socialization is beneficial for development, the current study highlights the need for further research to understand the impact of different socialization practices on kitten behavioural development, and the importance of accurately identifying when kittens are fearful and adapting socialization practices appropriately.

mcqs.q: In Graham et al. 2024, which factor was found to be the strongest predictor of fear behaviour towards unfamiliar people in foster kittens at adoption age (7–9 weeks)?
o: A) High exposure to cognitive enrichment-based non-social stimuli
B) Being reported fearful at intake into foster care
C) Low average social stimulus exposure
D) Foster parent having a low score for emotional stability
mcqs.e: The abstract states that 'kittens who were reported fearful at intake into foster care had significantly greater odds of displaying fear behaviours towards unfamiliar people and unfamiliar objects than kittens who were not reported fearful at intake.' This fearful-at-intake variable was also the only significant predictor for fear towards unfamiliar objects, making it the strongest overall predictor.

mcqs.q: According to Graham et al. 2024, what was the unexpected finding regarding cognitive enrichment-based non-social exposure (e.g., puzzle feeders, training, scent stimuli) during the kitten socialization period?
o: A) It significantly reduced fear towards both unfamiliar people and unfamiliar objects
B) It had no effect on fear behaviour in either social or non-social contexts
C) It was associated with greater odds of displaying fear towards unfamiliar people at adoption age
D) It reduced fear towards unfamiliar objects but not unfamiliar people
mcqs.e: The abstract states: 'kittens who received exposure to cognitive enrichment-based non-social stimuli had greater odds of displaying fear towards people compared to kittens who did not receive cognitive exposure.' The authors suggest this may represent flooding—exposure at high intensity that exceeds the kitten's ability to cope.

mcqs.q: Graham et al. 2024 used mixed logistic regression to examine risk factors for kitten fear behaviour. Which of the following correctly describes their finding about high social stimulus exposure?
o: A) High social exposure increased fear towards both people and objects
B) High social exposure had reduced odds of displaying fear towards unfamiliar people but was ineffective at reducing fear towards unfamiliar objects
C) High social exposure reduced fear towards unfamiliar objects but not unfamiliar people
D) Social exposure had no significant effect on fear behaviours in either context
mcqs.e: The abstract specifies: 'kittens who received high exposure to social stimuli had reduced odds of displaying fear towards people than kittens who received low social exposure, as predicted. High social exposure was ineffective at reducing fear levels towards unfamiliar objects.' This nuanced finding challenges blanket recommendations for high exposure during the socialization period.
